content_en:
Many CVs are never seen by a human. They get filtered out by ATS systems before a recruiter even has the chance to read them. In this guide, we explain how these systems work and how to optimize your application to get through.

## What is an ATS system?

ATS stands for Applicant Tracking System. It is software that companies use to:

- Receive and organize applications
- Search and filter candidates based on keywords
- Rank candidates by how well they match the job description
- Keep track of where candidates are in the process
- Communicate automatically with applicants

### Common ATS systems in Sweden
- Teamtailor (common in Swedish companies)
- Workday
- SAP SuccessFactors
- Taleo (Oracle)
- Greenhouse
- Lever
- ReachMee
- Varbi (public sector)

## How an ATS filters applications

### Step 1: Parsing (reading your CV)
The system reads your CV and pulls out information:
- Contact details
- Education
- Work experience
- Skills
- Keywords

**Problem:** If your CV has poor formatting, the system may miss or misread information.

### Step 2: Keyword matching
The system compares your CV against the requirements in the job ad:
- Exact keywords (for example, "project management")
- Synonyms (this varies between systems)
- Specific skills
- Education requirements
- Experience requirements

### Step 3: Ranking system
Candidates are ranked based on:
- Number of matching keywords
- Relevance of keywords (some count more than others)
- Length of experience
- Education level
- How well the profile matches the job requirements

### Step 4: Filtering
The recruiter can set thresholds:
- "Show only candidates with 80%+ match"
- "Exclude those without skill X"
- "Prioritize those with Y experience"

## Why CVs get filtered out

### 1. Wrong format
- An image-based PDF (a scanned document)
- Complex layouts with tables and columns
- Images, graphics, and icons
- Unusual fonts
- Text in headers and footers

### 2. Missing keywords
- Not using the exact words from the ad
- Abbreviations without the full term (or the other way around)
- Missing industry-specific terms
- Descriptions that are too generic

### 3. Wrong file format
- Word documents with compatibility issues
- Password-protected PDFs
- Images (JPG, PNG)
- Pages from portfolio tools

### 4. Structural problems
- Information that is not clearly separated
- Dates in unusual formats
- Headings the system doesn't recognize
- Mixing languages

## How to optimize your CV for an ATS

### Format and layout

**Use:**
- A simple, linear format (one column)
- Standard fonts (Arial, Calibri, Times New Roman)
- Clear headings: "Experience," "Education," "Skills"
- Bullet lists with simple bullet points
- A standard date format: "January 2022 – December 2024"

**Avoid:**
- Tables and columns
- Text boxes
- Graphics, icons, and images
- Headers and footers
- Creative layouts

### File format

**Best:**
- .docx (Word) – the most compatible
- .pdf (saved from Word, not scanned)

**Be careful with:**
- The older .doc format
- A PDF created from images
- Google Docs export (can look strange)

### Keyword optimization

**Step 1: Analyze the job ad**
Read the ad carefully and identify:
- Required qualifications (must-haves)
- Preferred qualifications (nice to have)
- Words and phrases that are repeated
- Specific systems, tools, certifications

**Step 2: Make a keyword list**
From the ad, pick out:
- Skills: "project management," "budget responsibility," "team leadership"
- Systems: "SAP," "Excel," "Salesforce"
- Traits: "analytical," "structured," "self-driven"
- Certifications: "PMP," "Agile," "ITIL"

**Step 3: Work them in naturally**
Don't stuff keywords in everywhere – work them in naturally:

❌ "Project management project management project manager project"

✅ "As a project manager, I was responsible for managing three parallel IT projects with a budget of SEK 5 million."

### Section headings an ATS understands

Use standard headings:
- **Contact Information** (or just your name at the top)
- **Summary** or **Profile**
- **Work Experience** or **Experience**
- **Education**
- **Skills**
- **Certifications** (if relevant)
- **Languages**

### Date format

Keep it consistent and clear:
- "January 2022 – December 2024"
- "Jan 2022 – Dec 2024"
- "2022-01 – 2024-12"

Avoid:
- "2022–present" written as just a dash (write "ongoing" or the current month instead)
- Using only the year for short jobs
- Inconsistent formats

### Skills section

List your skills in categories:

**Technical skills:**
Microsoft Excel (advanced), SAP, Salesforce CRM, Jira, Confluence

**Project methods:**
Agile, Scrum, PRINCE2, Waterfall

**Languages:**
Swedish (native), English (fluent), German (basic)

## ATS-friendly CV template

\`\`\`
FIRST NAME LAST NAME
Phone: 070-XXX XX XX | Email: name@email.com | LinkedIn: linkedin.com/in/name | City

SUMMARY
[2-3 sentences with keywords that match the job requirements]

WORK EXPERIENCE

Job Title | Company Name | City
Month Year – Month Year

• [Achievement with a measurable result and keywords]
• [Achievement with a measurable result and keywords]
• [Achievement with a measurable result and keywords]

Job Title | Company Name | City
Month Year – Month Year

• [Achievement with a measurable result and keywords]
• [Achievement with a measurable result and keywords]

EDUCATION

Degree/Program | School/University
Year – Year (or expected graduation year)

SKILLS

Technical: [List relevant technical skills]
Systems: [List relevant systems and tools]
Soft skills: [List relevant soft skills]
Languages: [List languages with level]

CERTIFICATIONS (optional)
[Certification], Issuer, Year
\`\`\`

## Test your CV

### Free ATS testing tools
- **Jobscan** (jobscan.co) – compares your CV against a job ad
- **Resume Worded** – AI-based feedback
- **SkillSyncer** – keyword analysis

### DIY test
1. Copy the text from your CV
2. Paste it into a blank text document (Notepad)
3. Can you read all the information correctly?
4. Is the structure preserved?
5. Is all the text included?

If the answer is yes to all of these, your CV is probably ATS-friendly.

## Balance the ATS and the human reader

Remember: the ATS is only the first hurdle. Your CV also needs to impress the recruiter.

### For the ATS:
- The right keywords
- The correct format
- A clear structure

### For the human reader:
- Sentences that tell a story
- Measurable results
- A personal touch
- Professional design (within the limits of being ATS-friendly)

### The two-CV strategy
Consider having:
1. **An ATS-optimized CV** – for online applications
2. **A nicely designed CV** – to bring to interviews or send directly

## Common myths about ATS

### Myth 1: "The ATS only reads the first page"
**Truth:** The ATS reads the entire document. But the recruiter might not.

### Myth 2: "I need an exact match on everything"
**Truth:** Most systems can handle synonyms and variations.

### Myth 3: "I can cheat by hiding keywords in white text"
**Truth:** Modern systems detect this, and it can disqualify you.

### Myth 4: "PDF never works"
**Truth:** Modern PDFs (created digitally, not scanned) usually work well.

### Myth 5: "An ATS doesn't understand career changers"
**Truth:** With the right keywords and clear transferable skills, it works.

## Checklist: Is your CV ATS-ready?

### Format
- [ ] Simple, linear format (one column)
- [ ] Standard fonts
- [ ] No tables or text boxes
- [ ] No images or graphics
- [ ] Saved as .docx or an ATS-friendly PDF

### Structure
- [ ] Clear standard headings
- [ ] Consistent date format
- [ ] Contact info at the top (not in a header)
- [ ] Readable as plain text

### Content
- [ ] Keywords from the job ad included
- [ ] Both abbreviations and full terms
- [ ] Measurable results and achievements
- [ ] Relevant skills listed

## Conclusion

ATS systems are not the enemy – they are tools that help recruiters handle large numbers of applications. By understanding how they work, you can adapt your CV so it gets through the automatic filtering AND impresses the recruiter once they read it.

The key is balance: technical optimization for the robot, and convincing content for the human.
summary_en: Understand how ATS systems (Applicant Tracking Systems) work, and how to optimize your CV to get noticed.
title_en: ATS Systems: How to Get Past the Robots

content_en:
The IT industry is one of the fastest-growing sectors, with high salaries and strong demand. Here is your guide to getting in and growing your career.

## Why IT and tech?

### Advantages
- **High salaries** – among the best-paid jobs
- **Strong demand** – there is a constant shortage of skilled people
- **Flexibility** – often the option to work remotely
- **Variety** – many different roles and specializations
- **Innovation** – you work with the technology of the future

### Challenges
- Fast pace of change – requires continuous learning
- Can be stressful in some roles
- Competition for the most attractive jobs
- Sometimes long working days near deadlines

## Common roles

### Developer/Programmer

**Frontend developer**
- Builds what users see (websites, apps)
- Technologies: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React, Vue
- Salary: 40,000–55,000 kr/month

**Backend developer**
- Builds servers, databases, and logic "behind the scenes"
- Technologies: Python, Java, Node.js, SQL
- Salary: 45,000–60,000 kr/month

**Full-stack developer**
- Knows both frontend and backend
- Salary: 45,000–65,000 kr/month

### UX/UI designer

**What you do:**
- Design user interfaces
- Research user behavior
- Create prototypes and wireframes
- Run user tests

**Tools:** Figma, Sketch, Adobe XD
**Salary:** 38,000–52,000 kr/month

### Project manager/Product manager

**What you do:**
- Lead IT projects
- Coordinate teams
- Prioritize features
- Communicate with stakeholders

**Salary:** 50,000–70,000 kr/month

### Data scientist/Analyst

**What you do:**
- Analyze large amounts of data
- Build AI/ML models
- Find insights and patterns
- Present results

**Tools:** Python, R, SQL, Tableau
**Salary:** 45,000–65,000 kr/month

### DevOps engineer

**What you do:**
- Automate and optimize development processes
- Manage cloud infrastructure
- Ensure system reliability

**Tools:** Docker, Kubernetes, AWS/Azure
**Salary:** 50,000–70,000 kr/month

### IT security specialist

**What you do:**
- Protect systems from intrusion
- Identify security risks
- Implement security solutions
- Handle incidents

**Salary:** 50,000–75,000 kr/month

## Paths to education

### Self-taught (completely possible!)
Many successful developers are self-taught:
1. Free courses online (freeCodeCamp, Codecademy)
2. YouTube tutorials
3. Your own projects (a portfolio)
4. Bootcamps (3-6 months, intensive)

### Yrkeshögskola (YH, vocational higher education)
- 1-2 years
- Includes an internship
- Closely linked to working life
- High employment rate after graduation

**Examples of programs:**
- Web developer
- Java developer
- IT security
- UX designer

### Högskola/University
- Computer engineering: 3-5 years
- Information systems: 3 years
- Interaction design: 3 years
- Data science: 2 years (master's)

### Certifications
Valuable certifications:
- AWS Certified (cloud services)
- Google Professional Certificate
- Microsoft Azure
- CISSP (security)
- Scrum/Agile

## Ways in without a formal education

### 1. Build a portfolio
- 3-5 projects that show your skills
- A GitHub profile with code
- Live demos of your projects
- Case studies of your process

### 2. Contribute to open source
- Show that you can collaborate
- Build contacts
- Learn from experienced developers

### 3. Take a bootcamp
- Intensive courses (3-6 months)
- Focus on practical skills
- Often comes with a job guarantee
- Costs money but moves quickly

### 4. Take a junior role or internship
- Start as a junior
- IT support as an entry point
- Internship through Arbetsförmedlingen (the Swedish Public Employment Service)

## Most in-demand skills

### Programming languages
1. JavaScript/TypeScript
2. Python
3. Java
4. C#
5. Go

### Frameworks and tools
1. React / Angular / Vue
2. Node.js
3. Docker / Kubernetes
4. Git
5. AWS / Azure / Google Cloud

### Soft skills
1. Problem-solving
2. Communication
3. Collaboration (agile teams)
4. Independence
5. Continuous learning

## Salary statistics

| Role | Junior | Average | Senior |
|------|--------|-------|--------|
| Frontend | 35,000 | 45,000 | 55,000+ |
| Backend | 38,000 | 50,000 | 65,000+ |
| Fullstack | 38,000 | 52,000 | 65,000+ |
| UX designer | 35,000 | 45,000 | 55,000+ |
| DevOps | 42,000 | 55,000 | 70,000+ |
| Data scientist | 40,000 | 52,000 | 70,000+ |

*Salaries vary depending on city, company, and experience*

## Employers

### Consulting companies
- HiQ, Sogeti, Accenture, Knowit
- Varied assignments
- Good for learning quickly
- Competitive salaries

### Product companies
- Spotify, Klarna, iZettle
- Work on their own product
- Often good benefits and culture
- High competition

### Startups
- Small companies in a growth phase
- Big influence, broad responsibility
- Risk, but also potential
- Often stock options

### Public sector
- Government agencies, regions, municipalities
- Security and work-life balance
- Meaningful work
- Often somewhat lower salaries

## Tips for success

### 1. Keep learning
IT changes fast – if you stop learning, you fall behind.
- Set aside time every week
- Follow industry news
- Take part in communities

### 2. Network
- Go to meetups and conferences
- Be active on LinkedIn
- Take part in online communities (Discord, Slack)

### 3. Build visibility
- Write a blog or technical articles
- Contribute to Stack Overflow
- Give presentations (even internal ones)

### 4. Specialize or broaden strategically
- Choose a niche and become an expert
- OR become "T-shaped" (a broad base plus one area of deep expertise)

## Future outlook

### Growing areas
- AI/Machine Learning
- Cybersecurity
- Cloud/DevOps
- Data Engineering
- AR/VR

### Forecast
- Demand will likely stay strong
- AI is changing the field but is not replacing developers
- Cloud services dominate
- Security is becoming more and more important

## Summary

The IT industry offers:
- High salaries and good conditions
- Many ways in (even without a university degree)
- Strong demand for skilled people
- Flexibility and variety

The key to success: stay curious, build things, and never stop learning!
summary_en: Career paths in IT – from developer to UX designer. What skills you need, salaries, and how to get started.

content_en:
The health and social care sector is one of Sweden's largest employers, with a constant need for staff. Here is everything you need to know to get started or grow in the industry.

## Why health and social care?

### Advantages
- **High demand** – a shortage occupation with many open jobs
- **Meaningful work** – you make a difference in people's lives
- **Secure employment** – the need does not go away
- **Many ways in** – different education levels
- **Career opportunities** – clear paths for development

### Challenges to be aware of
- Physically and mentally demanding
- Sometimes low staffing levels
- Irregular working hours are common
- Wages could be higher (but are improving)

## Common professions

### Nursing assistant (undersköterska)
**What you do:**
- Help patients with daily activities
- Take blood pressure and pulse
- Document and report
- Support nurses

**Education:** The Health and Social Care program (upper secondary school) or komvux (municipal adult education)
**Salary:** About SEK 28,000–32,000/month
**Demand:** Very high

### Nurse (sjuksköterska)
**What you do:**
- Carry out medical treatments
- Administer medication
- Lead nursing care
- Coordinate with doctors and others

**Education:** The nursing program (3 years at university)
**Salary:** About SEK 35,000–42,000/month
**Demand:** Very high

### Care assistant (vårdbiträde)
**What you do:**
- Support with daily activities
- Simpler care tasks
- Social support

**Education:** Shorter training or learned on the job
**Salary:** About SEK 25,000–28,000/month
**Demand:** High

### Personal assistant (personlig assistent)
**What you do:**
- Assist people with disabilities
- Enable an independent life
- Varied tasks

**Education:** No formal requirement, but courses are available
**Salary:** About SEK 25,000–30,000/month
**Demand:** High

### Specialist nurse (specialistsjuksköterska)
**What you do:**
- In-depth expertise in one area
- For example intensive care, anesthesia, psychiatry, pediatrics

**Education:** Nursing degree + specialist training (1-2 years)
**Salary:** About SEK 42,000–50,000/month
**Demand:** Very high

## Education paths

### The fastest way in
1. **Care assistant** – no formal education required
2. **SFI (Swedish for immigrants) + healthcare Swedish** – for those who learned Swedish as an adult
3. **Arbetsförmedlingen's (the Swedish Public Employment Service) training programs** – fast-track training to become a nursing assistant

### Upper secondary education
**The Health and Social Care program**
- 3 years
- Leads to a nursing assistant qualification
- Includes work placement (APL)

### Adult education (komvux)
- Nursing assistant training in 1-2 years
- Flexible format
- Possibility to combine with work

### University education
- Nurse: 3 years
- Occupational therapist: 3 years
- Physiotherapist: 3 years
- Doctor: 5.5 years + internship (AT)

### Yrkeshögskola (higher vocational education)
- Specialist nursing assistant
- Care administrator
- Medical office assistant

## Employers

### Public sector
- Regions (hospitals)
- Municipalities (elderly care, home care)

**Advantages:**
- Collective agreement
- Pension benefits
- Security

### Private sector
- Private healthcare companies
- Staffing agencies
- Private care homes

**Advantages:**
- Sometimes higher pay
- Flexibility
- Variety

## Career development

### Vertical development
1. Care assistant → Nursing assistant
2. Nursing assistant → Nurse
3. Nurse → Specialist nurse
4. Nurse → Manager/business developer

### Horizontal development
- Change workplace (hospital → home healthcare → psychiatry)
- Change patient group
- Move into teaching/supervision

### Niche areas
- Palliative care
- Dementia care
- Psychiatry
- Children and young people
- Addiction care

## Tips for getting into the industry

### If you lack education
1. Start as a substitute or hourly substitute
2. Take short courses (first aid, dementia care)
3. Apply for care assistant positions
4. Show commitment and learn on the job

### If you have a foreign education
1. Contact Socialstyrelsen (the National Board of Health and Welfare) for validation
2. Fill any gaps
3. Take language courses in healthcare Swedish
4. Do a work placement to get Swedish references

### Volunteer work
- Röda Korset (the Red Cross)
- Stadsmissionen (a Swedish charity organization)
- Volunteer organizations
- Gives you experience and references

## Salaries and benefits

### Salary statistics (monthly salary, SEK)
| Profession | Starting salary | Experienced |
|------------|------------------|--------------|
| Care assistant | 25,000 | 28,000 |
| Nursing assistant | 28,000 | 32,000 |
| Nurse | 35,000 | 42,000 |
| Specialist nurse | 42,000 | 50,000 |

### Benefits to negotiate
- OB pay (shift supplement for evenings/nights/weekends)
- Wellness allowance
- Pension
- Reduced working hours

## Future outlook

### Why demand is increasing
- The population is aging
- More people need care
- Retirements
- Expansion of welfare services

### Outlook 2024-2030
- Continued major staff shortage
- Rising pay levels (to attract staff)
- More technology and digitalization
- New ways of working (more home healthcare)

## Summary

Health and social care is an industry where:
- There are jobs to get
- You do meaningful work
- There are clear career paths
- Demand just keeps growing

Are you interested in working with people and want a secure career? Then health and social care could be right for you!
summary_en: A complete guide to a career in health and social care – education paths, professions, salaries, and future outlook.
title_en: Industry guide: Health and social care

content_en:
The labor market is changing fast. Some jobs disappear, new ones are created. Understanding the trends helps you make smart career choices.

## Drivers of change

### Technology
- **AI and automation** – Taking over routine tasks
- **Digitalization** – Changing how we work
- **New tools** – Requiring new skills

### Climate and sustainability
- **The green transition** – New industries are growing
- **Circular economy** – Changing business models
- **Regulations** – Affecting entire industries

### Demographics
- **An aging population** – Increased need for care
- **Urbanization** – Changing work patterns
- **Global competition** – Jobs are moving

### The legacy of the pandemic
- **Remote work** – A permanent change
- **E-commerce** – Continued growth
- **Focus on health** – New priorities

## Growing professions

### Tech and IT
- **AI/ML specialists** – Explosive demand
- **Cybersecurity** – Critical in the digital age
- **Cloud architects** – Companies are moving to the cloud
- **Data scientists** – Data is the new gold
- **DevOps engineers** – Faster delivery

### The green sector
- **Energy technicians** (solar, wind) – Needed for the transition
- **Sustainability strategists** – New legal requirements
- **Circular designers** – New business models
- **Electricians** (charging infrastructure) – The electric vehicle boom

### Healthcare and care
- **Nurses** – A chronic shortage
- **Doctors** – An aging population
- **Home care staff** – Elderly people living at home longer
- **Psychologists/therapists** – Mental health is a growing priority

### Other growing areas
- **E-commerce specialists**
- **Content creators**
- **HR tech / people analytics**
- **Robotics technicians**
- **Trainers / L&D (learning and development)**

## Professions under pressure

### At risk of automation
- **Cashiers** – Self-checkout, AI
- **Bookkeepers (routine tasks)** – Automation
- **Factory workers (simpler tasks)** – Robots
- **Telemarketers** – AI and chatbots
- **Bank tellers** – Digital services

### Structural changes
- **Fossil fuels** – Being phased out
- **Physical retail** – E-commerce
- **Traditional media** – Digitalization

### Note!
"At risk" does not mean "will disappear completely." It means:
- Fewer jobs overall
- Changed job duties
- A need for new skills

## Future-proof skills

### Technical skills
- Digital skills (at every level)
- Data analysis (basic knowledge)
- Understanding AI (as a user, not just as a developer)
- Programming (not just for programmers)

### Human skills (harder to automate)
- Creativity
- Critical thinking
- Emotional intelligence
- Leadership
- Complex problem-solving
- Communication

### Adaptability
- Ability to learn (more important than specific knowledge)
- Flexibility
- Resilience

## Strategies for the future

### 1. Continuous learning
- Update your skills regularly
- Take courses in new areas
- Stay curious

### 2. Combine disciplines
- T-shaped skills: a broad base plus deep expertise
- Unique combinations = a competitive advantage
- Tech skills + industry knowledge = valuable

### 3. Build your network
- Relationships survive change
- Stay in touch with your industry
- Be visible in your profession

### 4. Stay flexible
- Be open to lateral moves
- Think in terms of skills, not titles
- Adapt to the market

## If you're worried

### A historical perspective
Every technological revolution has created more jobs than it destroyed. ATMs did not replace bank tellers – they changed their job.

### What you can do today
1. Identify your transferable skills
2. Learn the basics of new technologies
3. Focus on what machines cannot do (creativity, empathy)
4. Build your network

### This won't disappear
Jobs that require:
- A physical presence
- Human contact
- Creativity
- Unpredictability
- Trust

## Summary

The future labor market rewards:
1. **Adaptability** – The ability to learn new things
2. **Technical understanding** – Not an expert, but capable
3. **Human skills** – What machines cannot do
4. **Specialization plus range** – T-shaped skills

Change is unavoidable. But with the right mindset, it is an opportunity, not a threat.
summary_en: AI, automation, and the shift to a greener economy are changing the labor market. Which jobs are disappearing, and which are being created?
title_en: Future Jobs – Which Careers Are Growing and Shrinking?

content_en:
Knowing the common interview questions and having prepared answers can make a real difference to your confidence.

The goal is not to memorize answers word for word — it shows, and it makes you sound stiff. The goal is to have thought through what you want to say, so you can say it in your own words even when you are nervous.

## About yourself

### "Tell me a bit about yourself"
A short version of your cover letter. Keep it professional, not personal.

Almost every interview starts here, and almost everyone answers for too long. Keep it to one or two minutes, in three parts: where you are now, what relevant things you have done, and why you are sitting there.

> "I have worked in warehouses for five years, most recently as a forklift driver at a distribution center. What I am best at is keeping a fast-moving flow organized. Now I want to work for you because you use the same system I already know, and I want a workplace with fixed hours."

Do not tell your life story starting from primary school. They are asking what kind of professional you are, not who you are as a person.

### "What are your strengths?"
Choose 2-3 strengths that are relevant to the job. Give concrete examples.

A strength without an example is just a claim. Name the strength, give the example, then connect it to the job — in that order.

### "What is your weakness?"
Choose something genuine that is not critical for the job. Show how you are working on it.

Avoid the answers that are really just disguised bragging ("I am too thorough," "I work too much"). Recruiters hear these every day, and they make you sound evasive. A real answer with an action attached is stronger:

> "I have found it hard to say no when I get too much on my plate, and it has made things stressful near the end. Now I check priorities with my manager right away when something new comes in, instead of saying yes and hoping for the best."

## About your background

### "Why did you leave your last job?"
Be positive and forward-looking. Never speak badly about a former employer.

This is true even when you were right. An interview is not the place to get justice — someone who complains about their former manager sounds like a future problem, no matter what actually happened. Keep it short and factual, and turn it toward the future.

### "Why is there a gap in your CV?"
Answer directly, without excuses, and move on. Illness, parental leave, caring for a family member, or unemployment are all common, and most recruiters have seen it before.

> "I was on sick leave for a year and have been fully recovered since spring. This fall, I took a course in bookkeeping to get started again."

You do not have to give a diagnosis or details about your health.

### "Tell me about a difficult situation at work"
Use the STAR method: Situation, Task, Action, Result.

**S** – what was the situation? **T** – what was your task? **A** – what did *you* do? **R** – what was the result?

The most common mistake is to get stuck on S and T and almost never reach A. A is what they want to hear — they are evaluating you, not the situation. Keep the background to two sentences.

## About the job

### "Why are you applying for this job specifically?"
Connect your goals and interests to what the company does.

Read the job ad again the evening before, and find two concrete things: something in the job duties you actually want to do, and something about the company that is not on the front page of their website.

### "Why should we hire you?"
This is your elevator pitch! Sum up what makes you unique.

## About the future

### "Where do you see yourself in 5 years?"
Show ambition, but be realistic. Focus on growing within the company.

This question is rarely about your dreams. It is about whether you will quit within a year. An answer that shows you want to become really good at this job is better than one that describes how quickly you want to move on.

### "What are your salary expectations?"
Have a number ready — not having one is a worse answer than a number that is slightly off. Check salary statistics for the job and the area before the interview, and give a range.

## Behavioral questions

"Tell me about a time when you..."
- handled a conflict
- made a mistake
- showed initiative

Prepare three or four stories from your work life and learn them well. The same story can often answer several different questions, depending on what you emphasize. This is much easier than trying to come up with an example on the spot.

## Questions you should ask

Not having any questions is almost always read as a lack of interest. Have three ready:

- "What do the first few months look like for the person who gets this job?"
- "What makes someone successful in this role?"
- "What happens next in the process, and when can I follow up?"

## About being nervous

Being nervous is expected, and it will not count against you. Two things help: arrive five minutes early so you have time to breathe, and bring notes. Looking at a piece of paper looks prepared, not unsure of yourself.

If you lose your train of thought, say so. "I lost my train of thought — can I start again?" is a completely normal thing to say, and it shows calm rather than the opposite.

## Remember

- Practice out loud! Say your answers out loud in front of a mirror
- Be honest – lies get discovered
- It is okay to pause and think
- Be yourself
summary_en: The most common interview questions, with suggested answers and strategies.

Many people underestimate what they can do. This guide helps you map all your skills so you can show employers your full value.

## Why do a skills inventory?

- You become aware of everything you can actually do
- You find skills you had forgotten about
- You get material for your CV and interviews
- You see which areas you can develop
- You gain more confidence

## Three types of skills

### 1. Formal skills
Documented qualifications:
- Education and degrees
- Certifications and licences
- Driving licences and forklift licences
- Language certificates
- Professional certificates

### 2. Practical skills
Skills you have learned through experience:
- Skills specific to your occupation
- Tools and systems you can use
- Methods and processes you know
- Technical skills

### 3. Personal skills (soft skills)
Your qualities and how you work:
- Communication skills
- Ability to collaborate
- Leadership
- Problem-solving
- Creativity

## Step by step: Make your inventory

### Step 1: List all your formal education

**Go through:**
- Upper secondary school (gymnasium)
- University or college
- Vocational training
- Komvux (municipal adult education) and folkhögskola (folk high school)
- Shorter courses and training
- Internal training from your employer
- Online courses and certifications

**Write down:**
| Education | Year | What did I learn? |
|------------|----|--------------------|
| Upper secondary school, Business | 2015 | Bookkeeping, Excel, business economics |
| Excel course through work | 2019 | Advanced formulas, pivot tables |

### Step 2: Document all your work experience

**Think broadly – include:**
- All jobs (even short ones)
- Internships
- Summer jobs
- Side jobs
- Volunteer work
- Board positions
- Family business

**For each experience, ask yourself:**
- What tasks did I have?
- What tools/systems did I use?
- What did I learn?
- What results did I achieve?

**Example:**
| Job | Tasks | Skills |
|------|-----------|-------------|
| Cashier at ICA | Checkout, restocking, customer service | Checkout systems, customer handling, handling stress |
| Football coach | Training sessions, matches, contact with parents | Leadership, planning, communication |

### Step 3: Identify hidden experience

Everyday activities that give you valuable skills:

**At home and in private life:**
- Renovated your home → Project management, craftsmanship
- Managed the family finances → Budgeting, financial understanding
- Organized parties/weddings → Event planning, coordination
- Cared for a sick family member → Care, patience, problem-solving

**Free time and volunteering:**
- Board work in an association → Administration, decision-making
- Coach/leader → Leadership, teaching skills
- Blogging/social media → Content creation, marketing
- Played in a band → Collaboration, creativity

**Travel and life experience:**
- Lived abroad → Languages, cultural understanding, adaptability
- Travelled on your own → Independence, problem-solving
- Moved to Sweden → Resilience, learning a new language, adapting

### Step 4: Identify your personal strengths

**Ask yourself:**
- What comes naturally to me?
- What do others ask me for help with?
- What do I often get praised for?
- What do I do without it feeling like effort?

**Common personal skills:**

| Skill | Example of how it shows |
|-----------|------------------------------|
| Communication | Explains things clearly, listens actively |
| Collaboration | Works well in a group, resolves conflicts |
| Problem-solving | Finds solutions, thinks creatively |
| Organization | Keeps things in order, plans effectively |
| Leadership | Takes initiative, motivates others |
| Adaptability | Handles change, learns quickly |
| Accuracy | Makes few mistakes, double-checks |
| Persistence | Does not give up, works toward long-term goals |

### Step 5: Categorize and prioritize

Sort your skills by:

**Relevance to the job you want:**
- Directly relevant (highlight first in your CV)
- Indirectly relevant (can be mentioned)
- Less relevant (leave out)

**Level:**
- Expert (can teach others)
- Experienced (works independently)
- Basic (needs some guidance)
- Beginner (needs supervision)

## Put together your skills document

Create a document you can use as a reference:

**Template:**

MY SKILLS

Formal qualifications:
- [Education 1]
- [Certification 1]
- [Driving licence/other licences]

Professional skills:
- [Skill 1] – [level] – [example]
- [Skill 2] – [level] – [example]

Tools and systems:
- [System 1] – [level]
- [Tool 1] – [level]

Personal strengths:
- [Strength 1] – [how it shows]
- [Strength 2] – [how it shows]

Languages:
- [Language 1] – [level]
- [Language 2] – [level]

## Use your inventory

### In your CV
- Choose the most relevant skills for each job
- Use concrete examples and results
- Match your wording to the job ad

### In your cover letter
- Highlight 2-3 key skills
- Connect them to the employer's needs

### In the interview
- Have an example ready for each skill
- Use the STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result)

## Common mistakes

- Underestimating everyday skills
- Forgetting old experiences
- Not asking others for input
- Only focusing on formal qualifications

## Remember

You can do more than you think! Take the time to really dig into your background – you will be pleasantly surprised.
summary_en: A guide to identifying all your skills – formal, practical, and personal.

A-kassa means unemployment insurance fund. It is an association that can pay you money if you lose your job. Here we explain how it works.

## What is a-kassa?

A-kassa is short for "arbetslöshetskassa" (unemployment insurance fund).

An a-kassa is an association. The association can pay you money if you become unemployed.

There are many different a-kassor (unemployment insurance funds). Most of them belong to a specific industry or profession.

## Are a-kassa and a union the same thing?

No. A-kassa and a union are two different things.

**The union** works for better conditions at work. For example, pay and rights.

**The a-kassa** is an insurance against unemployment. It can pay you money when you do not have a job.

You can be a member of a union without being a member of an a-kassa. You can be a member of an a-kassa without being a member of a union.

## Why should I join before I become unemployed?

If you are a member of an a-kassa for a while before you become unemployed, you can get more money.

If you wait to join, you may get less money, or nothing at all from that fund.

That is why it is good to join as soon as you get a job. Do not wait.

## Do I have to be a member to get any money at all?

No. There is a fund called Alfa-kassan. It is open to everyone, even if you have not been a member anywhere before.

If you have not been a member, you can still apply for money there. But the amount is often lower than if you had been a member for a while.

Always ask the a-kassa what applies to you.

## How do I become a member?

- Find an a-kassa that fits your profession. Not sure which one? Alfa-kassan accepts everyone.
- Go to the a-kassa's website.
- Apply for membership.
- Pay your fee every month.

## What should I do now?

Find an a-kassa that fits you and become a member as soon as you can. Do not wait until you lose your job.

Are you already unemployed? Contact an a-kassa anyway. Ask what applies to you.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does it cost money to be a member of an a-kassa?

Yes, you pay a fee every month. Ask your a-kassa how much it costs.

### Can I change a-kassa?

Yes. If you change profession, you may need to change a-kassa. Ask the a-kassa how to do it.
summary_en: What a-kassa means, why you should join before you become unemployed, and how to join.

Here are 10 tips to make your CV better. Follow them – and more employers will want to meet you!

## Tip 1: Write your name in large letters

Your name should be easy to see.
Write it at the top.
Use large text.

## Tip 2: Add your contact information

Write:
- Phone number
- Email
- Which city you live in

You do not need to write your full address.

## Tip 3: Most recent job first

Start with your most recent job.
Then the job before that.
This order is called "reverse chronological."

## Tip 4: Write what you did

Do not just tell WHERE you worked.
Tell WHAT you did.

**Bad example:**
"ICA Maxi, cashier"

**Good example:**
"ICA Maxi, cashier
- Helped customers at the checkout
- Restocked goods
- Answered questions"

## Tip 5: Use numbers

Numbers make your CV stronger.

**Bad:**
"I had many customers"

**Good:**
"I helped about 50 customers every day"

## Tip 6: Maximum two pages

Your CV should not be too long.
1-2 pages is enough.
Write the most important things.

## Tip 7: A simple layout

Use a simple design.
No strange colours.
No strange fonts.
It should be easy to read.

## Tip 8: No spelling mistakes

Spelling mistakes look unprofessional.
Read through it several times.
Ask someone else to read it too.

You can use spell check in Word.

## Tip 9: Adapt it to the job

Different jobs = different CVs.
Change it a little each time.
Highlight what fits the job.

If the job needs "customer service":
Write about your customer service experience.

## Tip 10: Save it the right way

Save it as a PDF.
Then it looks the same everywhere.
Name the file correctly:
"CV_Anna_Andersson.pdf"

## Summary

1. Name in large letters
2. Contact information
3. Most recent first
4. Tell what you did
5. Use numbers
6. Maximum 2 pages
7. Simple design
8. No spelling mistakes
9. Adapt it to the job
10. Save as a PDF

Follow these tips – and your CV will get better!
summary_en: Simple tips that make your CV better. Easy to understand and follow.
